# **Neuromorphic Vision for Counter-UAS: A Comprehensive Review of Event Camera-Based Drone Detection and Tracking**

The rapid proliferation of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), particularly highly agile multi-rotor drones, has introduced unprecedented challenges in airspace security, privacy, and safety. Traditional surveillance paradigms rely heavily on active sensors, such as radar, and passive standard optical cameras operating in the visible (RGB) or thermal spectra. However, the intrinsic characteristics of modern multi-rotor drones—namely their small radar cross-sections, low thermal signatures, extreme agility, and ability to operate in cluttered urban backgrounds—often render conventional detection systems inadequate1.  
Standard frame-based vision systems rely on Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) or Charge-Coupled Device (CCD) Active Pixel Sensors (APS). These sensors operate by capturing synchronous, dense matrices of pixel intensities at a fixed frame rate, typically utilizing a 3-transistor (3-T) cell with a reverse-bias photodiode that integrates light over an exposure period2. When tasked with tracking high-velocity drones, these systems suffer from fundamental physical limitations. The fixed integration time induces severe motion blur, low frame rates cause temporal aliasing, and their limited dynamic range (typically 60–70 dB) results in overexposure or underexposure in challenging lighting conditions, such as tracking a drone against the glare of the sun4. Furthermore, processing dense frames entails analyzing a massive volume of highly redundant static background data, which strains computational resources and increases system latency at the edge2.  
Event-based cameras, also known as Dynamic Vision Sensors (DVS) or neuromorphic cameras, represent a radical paradigm shift in visual perception inspired by biological retinas2. Rather than capturing global synchronous frames, an event camera consists of autonomous pixels that asynchronously report localized changes in logarithmic brightness2. When the intensity change at a specific pixel surpasses a defined threshold, the sensor outputs an event defined by the Address-Event Representation (AER) tuple ![][image1], where ![][image2] is the microsecond-resolution timestamp, ![][image3] are the spatial coordinates, and ![][image4] is the polarity indicating an increase or decrease in illumination8. This asynchronous, event-by-event operating principle fundamentally alters the data structure of computer vision. Event cameras effectively filter out static backgrounds, inherently isolating the dynamic target. They offer microsecond temporal resolution, eliminating motion blur even for high-velocity targets, and boast a high dynamic range exceeding 120 dB, enabling reliable operation across extreme lighting variations4.  
A substantial body of research has emerged detailing the application of these sensors for multi-rotor drone tracking. This report provides an exhaustive identification and analysis of the research papers, architectures, and datasets defining the current state of neuromorphic counter-UAV (C-UAV) technology.

## **The Physics of Neuromorphic Sensing: Propeller Signature Analysis**

One of the most robust and unique methodologies for identifying drones with event cameras is the analysis of the visual signature generated by their rapidly rotating propellers, as documented across several foundational papers1. Multi-rotor drone blades typically rotate at speeds ranging from 3,000 to 7,000 Revolutions Per Minute (RPM), corresponding to fundamental frequencies of 50 to 120 Hz7. For standard cameras, this rapid rotation results in an uninformative, transparent blur. However, for an event camera, the leading and trailing edges of the fast-moving blades generate a rich, high-frequency spatio-temporal pattern of events4. This periodic brightness change acts as a natural, uncooperative fiducial marker, distinguishing drones from other flying objects like birds or balloons, which exhibit fundamentally different kinematic event patterns4.  
![][image5]

### **Analytical Frequency-Domain Drone Detection**

The periodic motion of drone propellers can be modeled analytically to achieve robust, training-free detection. The core principle involves detecting the Blade-Pass Frequency (BPF) and its associated harmonic structures within the event stream8. When an event camera observes a spinning propeller, the idealized occlusion signal can be mathematically represented as a periodic pulse train. Because this signal is periodic, its power spectrum consists of impulses at integer multiples (harmonics) of the fundamental BPF8.  
In the research paper "A Virtual Fence for Drones: Efficiently Detecting Propeller Blades with a DVXplorer Event Camera," Stewart et al. detail a temporal histogram methodology that identifies these harmonic peaks11. Their system calculates the time elapsed between sequential ON and OFF events at each individual pixel. By accumulating these period measurements in a temporal histogram—utilizing highly efficient bit-shifting operations with 256 bins of 128 microseconds each—the system identifies distinct peaks at the primary propeller frequency and its sub-harmonics11. These sub-harmonics manifest because the event camera may probabilistically miss rapid illumination transitions due to bandwidth saturation or contrast threshold limitations. The authors successfully paired this algorithm with a small 100-neuron classifier network running at 100 Hz to detect drones at extended ranges (up to 19 meters) with 98% accuracy, effectively functioning as a low-power neuromorphic virtual tripwire11.  
More advanced frequency-domain techniques rely on direct per-pixel frequency analysis without requiring temporal binning. In "Real-Time Drone Detection in Event Cameras via Per-Pixel Frequency Analysis," the authors introduce the DDHF framework, which leverages the Non-Uniform Discrete Fourier Transform (NDFT) directly on the asynchronous timestamps8. By computing the power spectrum of the asynchronous event series, the system captures periodic structures directly. To reject noise generated by random background motion or sensor hot-pixels, the DDHF framework employs spectral flatness metrics. Background noise typically produces a uniform, flat spectral response, whereas the periodic motion of a rotor yields a concentrated "comb-like" harmonic structure8. By setting a threshold to discard spectra with high spectral flatness, the algorithm efficiently filters out distractors and detects drones at ranges up to 300 meters, successfully addressing edge cases such as stationary hovering drones that would evade standard optical flow motion trackers8.

### **Event-Based Tachometry and State Estimation**

Beyond simple detection, the rich temporal data from propellers enables precise event-based tachometry—measuring the rotational speed of the drone's motors in real-time. The papers "Event-Based Angular Speed Measurement (EB-ASM)" and "EV-Tach" establish paradigms for estimating propeller rotational speed with high fidelity7. These systems process the elapsed time between localized event bursts to calculate angular displacement. Such event-based tachometers have demonstrated remarkable fidelity, achieving relative error rates below 0.2%—performance comparable to commercial laser tachometers, but with the distinct advantage of operating passively, across multiple propellers simultaneously, and under challenging lighting4.  
Crucially, the rotational speeds of the individual propellers serve as a direct proxy for the drone's internal flight dynamics. In the paper "Count Every Rotation and Every Rotation Counts: Exploring Drone Dynamics via Propeller Sensing," Wang et al. introduce EventPro, a system that exploits these speeds7. Because the thrust (![][image6]) and torque (![][image7]) of a multi-rotor drone scale proportionally with the square of the propeller's angular velocity (![][image8]), EventPro uses Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) encoder-decoder models to reverse-engineer the drone's internal control commands (e.g., hover, pitch, roll, yaw, climb) from the raw event stream13. Furthermore, by fitting geometric shapes (like ellipses) to the aggregated point cloud generated by a propeller, researchers can independently estimate the drone's attitude relative to the camera, establishing propeller signature analysis as a comprehensive tool for uncooperative target state estimation4.

### **Generative Learning: EVPropNet**

While analytical methods are highly effective, learning-based approaches have further extended the capabilities of propeller tracking, specifically addressing the historic lack of annotated event data. In the seminal paper "EVPropNet: Detecting Drones By Finding Propellers For Mid-Air Landing And Following," Sanket et al. bypass the need for physical data collection by developing a geometric simulation of propeller blades15. By projecting a simplified geometric model—using cubic basis splines—onto a virtual image plane, the authors applied an Event Generation Model (EGM). The EGM simulates an event trigger when the logarithmic intensity change ![][image9] crosses a defined contrast threshold16.  
A deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained purely on this massive synthetic dataset of propeller events demonstrated the unprecedented ability to transfer seamlessly to real-world event streams without fine-tuning4. EVPropNet has successfully enabled complex autonomous robotics applications, including tracking an unmarked moving quadrotor with a 92% success rate, and executing precise mid-air docking and landing on flying quadrotors using purely onboard edge computation15.

## **Evolution of Drone-Centric Event Datasets**

The advancement of learning-based event vision was historically bottlenecked by a severe lack of annotated data. Early event datasets were primarily focused on autonomous driving or simple indoor environments. Drones present a unique challenge: they are highly unconstrained in 6-DOF space, routinely undergo scale changes, and frequently occupy only a tiny fraction of the sensor's field of view. In recent years, the research community has rapidly addressed this gap, establishing robust benchmarks to evaluate detection and tracking algorithms. The defining papers and datasets in this domain demonstrate a clear progression from low-resolution, single-modality indoor sets to massive, high-definition, multimodal benchmarks operating in extreme environments.

![][image10]  
As demonstrated in the comparison, early works like the one by Iaboni et al. established baseline viability for tracking multiple quadrotors, but modern research demands higher complexity18. The FRED (Florence RGB-Event Drone) dataset explicitly targets this complexity by providing benchmarks for tracking and trajectory forecasting in adverse conditions where visible light cameras fail entirely24. Concurrently, datasets like EV-UAV focus specifically on the "tiny object" problem, providing a rigorous benchmark for networks that must identify drones represented by only a handful of sparsely distributed event pixels at extreme ranges4.

## **Deep Learning Architectures: Dense vs. Sparse Event Processing**

The primary challenge in applying deep learning to event camera data lies in the sensor's asynchronous output format. Standard computer vision architectures (like CNNs or Vision Transformers) rely on dense, synchronous matrices of data. Directly feeding them sparse, time-continuous event streams is highly inefficient. To solve this, researchers in drone detection have developed three primary data representation and architectural paradigms: Dense Spatio-Temporal Representations, Fully Sparse Point Cloud Processing, and Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)4.

### **Dense Spatio-Temporal Representations**

The most straightforward method to leverage existing computer vision architectures involves converting event streams into dense surrogate representations. A common approach accumulates events over a fixed temporal window to create 2D event frames or temporal histograms4. While this enables the immediate use of mature, highly optimized models like YOLOv5 or YOLOv8, it introduces fundamental flaws. Aggregating events over time artificially reintroduces a frame rate, thereby destroying the microsecond temporal resolution that is the event camera's primary advantage, ultimately inducing motion blur on highly agile targets like drones4. Furthermore, dense event frames process empty background pixels, wasting computational resources25.  
A more sophisticated dense approach utilizes 3D Voxel Grids. As detailed in tracking papers like "EventVOT," the spatio-temporal volume of the event stream is discretized into a regular 3D structure4. The 2D sensor plane is extended along the temporal axis, which is partitioned into bins. Each voxel encodes the polarity and density of events occurring at a given pixel location during a specific temporal interval4. This representation preserves temporal dynamics more explicitly than flattened frames and provides a highly structured input suitable for 3D CNNs and optical flow algorithms4.

### **Fully Sparse and Point Cloud Processing**

Recognizing the computational inefficiency of converting sparse events into dense tensors, modern architectures increasingly treat event streams natively as time-continuous 3D point clouds ![][image11].  
In the paper "Event-based Tiny Object Detection: A Benchmark Dataset and Baseline," Chen et al. introduce EV-SpSegNet, a network specifically designed for tiny drone detection4. At long distances, drones appear merely as small, continuous curves in the spatio-temporal event point cloud. EV-SpSegNet utilizes a Grouped Dilated Sparse Convolution Attention (GDSCA) module to process these points natively4. By extracting multi-scale local and long-range features, the network identifies these distinctive curve-like trajectories. Complementing this is the Spatiotemporal Correlation (STC) Loss function, which specifically promotes event continuity and penalizes isolated background noise, drastically enhancing the network's ability to segment tiny drones from clutter4.  
Similarly, the classification of uncooperative flying objects—distinguishing multi-rotor drones from biological distractors like birds or insects—has been achieved using architectures like PointNet and PointNet++4. These networks directly consume the event point cloud and learn the implicit kinematic signatures inherent in the data, seamlessly differentiating the rigid, high-frequency mechanical vibration of a drone from the organic, lower-frequency flapping of a bird4.  
The apex of this sparse methodology is documented in the 2026 paper "No Dense Tensors Needed: Fully Sparse Object Detection on Event-Camera Voxel Grids" by Sadoun et al., introducing SparseVoxelDet25. By restricting computation exclusively to active spatial positions—which frequently constitute less than 1% of the 3D voxel grid—SparseVoxelDet prevents dense feature map construction entirely25. Evaluated on the FRED drone dataset, the model achieved state-of-the-art mAP scores while processing only \~14,900 active voxels per frame. This fully sparse paradigm yielded an 858x reduction in GPU memory footprint and a 3,670x reduction in storage compared to dense equivalents, proving that computational cost can scale directly with scene activity rather than physical sensor resolution25.

## **Multimodal Sensor Fusion Strategies**

While event cameras possess extraordinary capabilities for motion detection and high dynamic range, they are not without limitations. Standard contrast DVS sensors do not capture absolute intensity or color, which can hamper semantic identification of static objects. Furthermore, while they excel at detecting transverse motion, their ability to estimate absolute distance is poor without active stereo setups or complex ego-motion calculations31. To construct highly reliable counter-UAV systems, researchers have developed advanced multimodal fusion networks.

| Fusion Modality | Associated Architecture / Paper | Primary Advantages | Fusion Mechanism / Loss Strategy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **RGB \+ Event** | ER-DETR (Magrini et al., NeRDD)23 | Merges dense semantic texture (RGB) with high-temporal motion cues (Event). Overcomes RGB motion blur. | Asymmetric Modality Injection (Cross-attention transformer) with Hungarian set matching loss. |
| **RGB \+ Event** | SMG-UAV (Zhang et al.)32 | Excels at small-target detection in extreme illumination by suppressing unreliable responses from degraded RGB frames. | Sparse Mutual Guided Bridge fusing CNN (RGB) features with LIF spiking neuron (Event) features. |
| **Radar \+ Event** | RVT-Tiny / DVS-Radar Fusion31 | Provides absolute distance (Radar) and operates flawlessly in all weather/total darkness while tracking micro-movements (Event). | Recurrent Transformer modeling; leverages time-history to maintain track during stationary periods. |
| **Radar \+ Event** | Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) / ADFM34 | Quantifies sensor uncertainty, ensuring detection is based on strong evidence rather than out-of-distribution noise. | Dempster-Shafer theory; feature-level fusion via Adaptive Dynamic Fusion Modules (ADFM). |

### **RGB-Event Fusion**

The most common pairing combines an event camera with a standard optical RGB camera. RGB provides rich semantic textures and contextual awareness for static or slow-moving targets in adequate lighting, while event cameras compensate during high-speed maneuvers or in High Dynamic Range (HDR) conditions23.  
In the development of the NeRDD dataset, researchers adapted the DEtection TRansformer (DETR) architecture into an RGB-Event tracker (ER-DETR)23. Standard DETR operates via bipartite matching using a Hungarian loss function, which inherently removes the need for Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)23. To fuse the modalities, researchers utilized a technique called *asymmetric modality injection*. In this setup, information from one domain (e.g., RGB) is projected into a query matrix in a cross-attention transformer layer, while the complementary domain (e.g., Event) generates the keys and values23. This allows the network to utilize appearance tokens to attend to high-temporal motion tokens, seamlessly fusing them via skip-connections. Consequently, the network successfully highlights drones against cluttered backgrounds where RGB algorithms alone completely fail23.  
Another prominent architecture is SMG-UAV (Sparse Mutual Guided RGB-Event Fusion)32. This network addresses the disparity between dense RGB semantics and sparse event spikes. SMG-UAV processes the modalities through separate backbones. Crucially, the event branch utilizes biological Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons to inherently map the sparse temporal motion cues32. A Sparse Mutual Guided Bridge then aligns these outputs, explicitly suppressing unreliable responses from either sensor—for example, mitigating severe RGB motion blur using the sharp kinematic edges provided by the event branch32.  
![][image12]

### **Radar-Event Fusion**

For genuine all-weather, long-range anti-UAV systems, optical capabilities must be fused with radio frequency technologies, specifically 77 GHz mmWave or Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar. Radar excels at providing absolute distance and radial velocity (via the Doppler shift) and operates flawlessly in fog, rain, or complete darkness31. However, radar suffers from low angular resolution and can be highly confused by ground clutter and multi-path reflections.  
Fusing radar with an event camera creates a highly synergistic perception stack. Research utilizing recurrent transformer architectures, such as RVT-Tiny, on combined DVS and radar data has demonstrated substantial improvements, achieving up to 47.5% mAP with mean absolute radar distance errors below 1.8 meters against LiDAR ground truths31. The temporal modeling inherent in recurrent networks proves essential; the network learns to leverage the radar's distance and the event camera's microsecond angular motion history simultaneously, effectively tracking targets even during brief stationary periods where optical motion-based detection would fail31. Furthermore, to manage the inherent noise of radar and DVS sensors, evidential deep learning frameworks utilizing Dempster-Shafer theory have been introduced. These frameworks utilize Adaptive Dynamic Fusion Modules (ADFM) at the feature level to quantify the epistemic uncertainty of each sensor, ensuring that drone predictions are backed by strong multimodal evidence rather than out-of-distribution noise34.

## **Biologically Inspired Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)**

While deep learning provides powerful tools, the most philosophically and mathematically aligned method for processing neuromorphic event data is the Spiking Neural Network (SNN)36. Unlike standard Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) that communicate via continuous, synchronous floating-point activations, SNNs use discrete, binary spikes, closely mimicking the biological architecture of the human brain's dendrites, soma, and axons36.  
The fundamental computational unit of an SNN is often the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model. In this model, the neuron maintains an internal membrane potential (![][image13]) governed by differential equations. The potential integrates incoming spikes over time and naturally leaks back to a resting state (![][image14])37. When the potential crosses a dynamic threshold, the soma generates an action potential (a spike) that propagates down the axon to connected neurons37.  
SNNs excel in C-UAV applications for two distinct reasons. First, they natively accept asynchronous event data via various encoding schemes (such as Poisson Encoding, where firing rate is proportional to intensity, or Intensity-to-Latency encoding, where brighter pixels fire earlier) without requiring artificial time-binning37. Second, they offer extraordinary power efficiency when deployed on dedicated neuromorphic hardware, due to the extreme spatial and temporal sparsity of the spike trains.

### **Neuromorphic Edge Deployment**

For drone detection at the edge, where Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) constraints are severe, SNNs have been successfully deployed on specialized chips. Intel's Loihi 2 processor, for example, supports advanced neuron models like the Sigma-Delta Neural Network (SDNN). In drone tracking experiments (such as the PilotNet SDNN implementation), Loihi 2 achieved energy consumption as low as 1.06 mJ per frame and latencies of 1.13 ms (operating at over 442 FPS), demonstrating a massively superior energy-delay product compared to traditional edge GPUs39. Similar efficiencies were noted in event-based car classification (CarSNN) on Loihi40.  
Another leading hardware platform is the SynSense Speck. The Speck is a "sensing-computing integrated" System-on-Chip (SoC) that physically bonds a 128x128 pixel Dynamic Vision Sensor array directly to a DYNAP-CNN spiking processor containing over 330,000 neurons41. This architecture creates a fully asynchronous pipeline where events never leave the chip to access external memory. As detailed in "Drone Detection Using a Low-Power Neuromorphic Virtual Tripwire," SNNs deployed on the Speck chip can perform complex binary drone classification with latencies under 5 milliseconds while consuming less than 2 milliwatts of power—an efficiency impossible to achieve with traditional frame-based cameras and Von Neumann processors41.  
To push the boundaries of accuracy while maintaining SNN efficiency, researchers have developed complex hybrid architectures such as the Spiking Swin Transformer. This architecture merges the hierarchical, long-range self-attention mechanisms of Transformers with the event-driven energy efficiency of spiking neurons, establishing new state-of-the-art baselines for robust UAV detection under extreme power constraints1.

## **Trajectory Forecasting and Edge Operations**

Detecting and tracking a drone is fundamentally reactive; anticipating its future path is a proactive necessity for interception, jamming, or automated evasion (detect-and-avoid) operations.

### **Event-Based Trajectory Forecasting**

Traditional trajectory forecasting algorithms struggle with the non-linear, high-agility maneuvers characteristic of multi-rotor quadrotors. In the event domain, hybrid models like Residual Kalman Dynamics (RKD) have shown exceptional promise, as detailed by Nyblom et al.46. The RKD architecture intelligently integrates classical filtering theory with deep learning. First, an optimized constant-velocity Kalman filter establishes a stable physical baseline using the full center-size bounding box state derived from the event stream. A neural network head is then trained to predict the high-frequency *acceleration residuals*—the nonlinear deviations—on top of this Kalman state based on the historical event stream46. This separation of reliable physical priors from learned complex dynamics improves both short-horizon (400 ms) and mid-horizon (800 ms) bounding box forecasts on datasets like FRED, allowing the system to accurately predict drone positions through aggressive evasive maneuvers where simple linear extrapolation entirely fails46.  
For drone-mounted operations (ego-motion tracking), the FlyTracker system demonstrates how a monocular event camera carried by a drone can track its own motion while simultaneously detecting moving obstacles in its field of view10. By utilizing an online background-subtraction method based on the Event Generation Model, FlyTracker fuses photometric features to maintain robust tracking in dynamic environments10.

### **Operational Challenges: Bias Tuning and System Integration**

Deploying event cameras in uncontrolled outdoor environments introduces significant analog operational challenges. Specifically, the sensitivity and signal-to-noise ratio of an event camera are governed by hardware bias parameters. These biases control the pixel's sensitivity to contrast changes (thresholds), its internal low-pass filter (bandwidth), and its refractory period (the mandatory rest time between spikes)47.  
Improper tuning of these biases in bright sunlight, or when observing highly reflective propellers, can lead to immediate bandwidth saturation. When saturated, the sensor generates an overwhelming volume of noise events, effectively destroying the high-frequency temporal signature of the drone11. To combat this, automated tuning frameworks like BiasBench are increasingly utilized. These frameworks employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms to dynamically adjust analog biases in real-time based on scene illumination and motion dynamics, ensuring optimal contrast thresholds and preventing data bottlenecks in the tracking pipeline17.  
When custom neuromorphic chips (like Speck or Loihi) are unavailable, field deployments frequently utilize heterogeneous System-on-Chip (SoC) architectures, such as the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX or Jetson Xavier. The F-UAV-D research explicitly profiled these systems, demonstrating that optimized YOLOv8 architectures can process dense event frames in real-time (under 50 ms latency) while maintaining total system power consumption below 15 watts4. Additionally, Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are heavily utilized to implement custom asynchronous routing protocols for event streams, providing a resilient foundation for real-time motion estimation in embedded C-UAV deployments51.

## **Conclusion**

The integration of neuromorphic vision into multi-rotor drone detection and tracking systems marks a fundamental and necessary departure from traditional spatial imaging. By leveraging dynamic vision sensors that respond exclusively to asynchronous changes in illumination, researchers have bypassed the limitations of motion blur, low dynamic range, and temporal aliasing that severely handicap conventional radar and optical surveillance systems.  
The evolution of this field is distinct and rapidly accelerating. It began with elegant, algorithmic frequency-comb filtering designed to isolate the high-frequency microsecond signatures of rotating propeller blades, enabling highly precise event-based tachometry. It has since scaled into massive, multimodal deep-learning networks that fuse sparse event point-clouds with dense RGB semantics and FMCW radar ranging. Supported by robust new benchmarks—ranging from the multimodal extremes of FRED to the dense semantic annotations of ES-UAV—and propelled by advancements in fully sparse architectures (like SparseVoxelDet) and dedicated Spiking Neural Network hardware, event-based C-UAV systems are transitioning from laboratory novelties to deployable, low-SWaP edge technology. The unique capacity of event cameras to not only detect the spatial presence of a drone, but to accurately estimate its motor speeds, infer its flight dynamics, and forecast its nonlinear trajectory, unequivocally positions neuromorphic engineering as a cornerstone technology for the future of secure airspace management.
